{"id": "92:9/q05", "question": "What occasion or illustrative event is reported for these verses?", "turns_on": "The reports differ in the people, transaction and price, or the time of the angels' call.", "positions": [{"id": "92:9/q05/p1", "position": "A miserly palm owner denied fallen dates to a poor household; a believer exchanged forty palms for that tree and gave it to them.", "reasons": "Ibn Abi Hatim's Ibn Abbas report says the buyer was promised a palm in Paradise; it links the surah's revelation to this sale."}, {"id": "92:9/q05/p2", "position": "A palm owner refused a Paradise palm in exchange; Abu al-Dahdah bought his tree and donated it to the needy neighbor.", "reasons": "Ata's accounts in al-Tha'labi and al-Baghawi differ in purchase detail: al-Baghawi says he paid with his garden, while al-Tha'labi only says he bought it. Ibn ʿĀshūr and Ibn ʿAṭiyya describe gradual or continuing involvement in deeds, and al-Alūsī explicitly prefers preparation for obedience or disobedience with their dispositions. {"id": "92:10/q13", "question": "How does the verse relate to its surrounding verses and the sūra?", "turns_on": "Whether the connection concerns the mirrored clauses, the later Fire image, the preceding sūra, or other verses.", "positions": [{"id": "92:10/q13/p1", "position": "It completes the second half of a structured contrast between conduct and recompense.", "reasons": "Al-Irshād says giving and withholding lead their clauses because they ground subsequent piety, belief, denial, or self-sufficiency. {"id": "92:10/q14", "question": "What does the contrasting easy course denote?", "turns_on": "Whether the easier counterpart means a beneficial condition generally or Paradise specifically.", "positions": [{"id": "92:10/q14/p1", "position": "It is a good and pleasing condition, broadly what benefits or suits a person without hardship.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya places the condition in this life and the next; Ibn ʿĀshūr says the feminine form may mark an afterlife condition or place and broadens the sense to what suits its possessor."}, {"id": "92:10/q14/p2", "position": "It denotes Paradise.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr reports this from Zayd ibn Aslam and Mujāhid."}]}

{"id": "92:10/q16", "question": "What conduct characterizes the miser in this contrast?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "92:10/q16/p1", "position": "He withholds God's due, considers himself self-sufficient, and denies the promise.", "reasons": "Al-Durr reports this explanation from Qatāda, paired with the giver who pays God's due, avoids prohibitions, and believes the promise."}]}

{"id": "92:11/q03", "question": "Why is 'idhā' used for the fall?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "92:11/q03/p1", "position": "It marks the fall as certain or recurrent, making the warning unavoidable.", "reasons": "Al-Sāmarrāʾī compares certain events introduced by idhā—death, the end of sacred months, sunrise, and completed prayer, citing 5:106, 9:5, 18:17, and 62:10. {"id": "92:11/q05", "question": "How does the wording of verse 11 connect to verse 10?", "turns_on": "The notes range from the immediate link to the hard path in verse 10 to the larger contrast between the surah's two paths.", "positions": [{"id": "92:11/q05/p1", "position": "It continues the promise of facilitation to the hard path and shows its end: Hell, where the miser's wealth cannot save him.", "reasons": "Tustarī says God enables the deeds of Hell. {"id": "92:11/q06", "question": "Does verse 11 close the account of the wicked or begin the next theological statement?", "turns_on": "The pronoun and ġ-n-y echo point backward, while Neuwirth's classification groups the verse with the following theological lines.", "positions": [{"id": "92:11/q06/p1", "position": "It belongs to the wicked person's section.", "reasons": "Corpus Coranicum prefers this because 'him' refers back to the wicked person, the root ġ-n-y echoes verse 8, and inna starts a fresh statement at verse 12; the result is a structural asymmetry."}, {"id": "92:11/q06/p2", "position": "It belongs with the theological predication of verses 12–13.", "reasons": "Corpus Coranicum reports Neuwirth's classification."}]}
{"id": "92:11/q07", "question": "How does verse 11 fit the surah's wider arrangement?", "turns_on": "Different notes analyze the mirror pattern, the relation to the previous surah, and the move to the final outcomes.", "positions": [{"id": "92:11/q07/p1", "position": "The surah mirrors two groups, reversing the order of salvation and damnation in its final stanza.", "reasons": "Corpus Coranicum says the outer blessed sections are joined by ittaqā in verse 5 and atqā in verse 17; the earlier lists of conduct precede reward or warning, while the last stanza gives warning and promise before conduct."}, {"id": "92:11/q07/p2", "position": "The oath and its response situate differing human efforts and the failure of wealth within the surah's relation to the preceding surah.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr contrasts the previous surah's oath by the shaped soul, intellect, and knowledge with this surah's oath by the body and its sexes; the response says human striving differs and emphasizes wealth's failure at the fall."}, {"id": "92:11/q07/p3", "position": "The section after this verse states the just and inevitable ends of both groups.", "reasons": "Quṭb says the next section first establishes that both outcomes are just, true, and inevitable."}]}

{"id": "92:12/q01", "question": "Why is the assertion emphatic?", "turns_on": "Which objection the emphatic wording is understood to answer.", "positions": [{"id": "92:12/q01/p1", "position": "The emphatic particles answer the objection that God would have compelled everyone to believe if He wished.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr says the imagined objection excuses idolatry and cites 43:20."}, {"id": "92:12/q01/p2", "position": "The emphasis counters people's rejection of God's guidance and their claim to define guidance themselves.", "reasons": "Al-Sāmarrāʾī cites the rarity of belief in 12:103 and the misleading majority in 6:116; the emphasis strengthens both the exclusive source and the path's destination."}]}

{"id": "92:12/q06", "question": "How do divine guidance and human choice relate?", "turns_on": "Whether guidance only discloses a choice, produces obedience, or brings a person to the end; and how human inclination is understood.", "positions": [{"id": "92:12/q06/p1", "position": "God shows the path and enables discernment; people choose whether to accept and follow it.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya says everyone receives perception, then acquires what is allotted; guidance into faith for all would leave no unbelievers.
